newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Russian premier begins Czech visit with local beer.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier begins Czech visit with local beer.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, beginning a visit to the Czech Republic expected to include tough talking on NATO expansion, on Sunday toured an engineering works and sampled local beer.
Chernomyrdin travelled to Plzen, 80 km (50 miles) west of Prague to visit the headquarters of Skoda a.s., whose output includes railway locomotives, power turbines and drink cans.
After a tour of the sprawling plant, Chernomyrdin took the wheel of one of the Skoda group's Tatra limousines and tasted the Pilsner beer brewed in the city.

Asked what would be the main topic of his talks with Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus on Monday, Chernomyrdin told reporters: "It will be above all the economy. We have to resolve some problems. But there will be a whole complex of other questions."
Klaus was quoted by CTK news agency after meeting Chernomyrdin at Prague airport as saying that apart from the economy, wider international questions would be discussed.
"We have to clarify some foreign policy questions at the highest level," he said.

Russian officials have said the talks will cover Moscow's opposition to the eastward expanion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO), which the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are leading contenders to join.
The Czechs, while saying Russian security concerns should be taken into account, say NATO expansion is unstoppable.

Moscow wants a binding agreement with NATO that the alliance will not deploy new troops or weapons in former Soviet bloc countries. But NATO is against any deal which would risk consigning new members to second-class participation.

Russian ambassador to Prague Nikolai Ryabov, who accompanied Chernomyrdin to Plzen, angered Czech officials earlier this year when he said key bilateral agreements could be jeopardised if the Czechs joined NATO.

Prague earlier this month signed a landmark deal with Norwegian gas suppliers, under which the Czechs would import 53 billion cubic metres of gas over 20 years, breaking the Czech Republic's dependency on Russian gas.

Russian monopoly gas supplier Gazprom attacked the deal with Norway and Chernomyrdin is likely to raise Moscow's hopes to seal a new long-term supply contract once the current one with the Czech Republic expires in 1998.
Skoda, Gazprom and Russian company Lyulka Saturn said in March they were planning to set up as joint venture to produce gas turbines.
Asked if politicians could help boost Russian-Czech trade ties, Chernomyrdin said, "I would very much like politics not to interfere. We should create conditions for entrepreneurs."
Chernomyrdin is due to leave Prague early on Tuesday.
